source.title: NaViL: Rethinking Scaling Properties of Native Multimodal Large Language Models under Data Constraints
source.authors: Chang-Yao Tian; Hao Li; G. Luo; Xi-Zhou Zhu; Weijie Su; Han-Ming Deng; Jin-Guo Zhu; Jie Shao; Ziran Zhu; Yunpeng Liu; Lewei Lu; Wen-Hai Wang; Hong-Sheng Li; Ji-Feng Dai

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Studies scaling in native multimodal models, extending loss-scaling measurements to a visual-language training setting.
record.gate_note: The paper measures validation teacher-forcing loss while varying model size, training data, and visual-encoder architecture. It also reports downstream benchmark scores, but those comparisons do not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. Cited scaling-law results are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out multimodal teacher-forcing loss while scaling LLM size (0.5B–7B), visual-encoder size (75M–2.4B) and data (15M–120M pairs), and varies encoder depth and width at a fixed 600M parameters. This is a new (native image-text) setting with its own loss results, bearing on V5 and V4. It is not text-LM pretraining, so V1 itself is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LLM initialization plus MoE greatly help native MLLMs under data constraints. LLM scaling follows the usual LLM scaling-law pattern, while visual-encoder gains are capped by LLM capacity. Optimal encoder size grows log-linearly with LLM size. NaViL-2B/9B are competitive with compositional MLLMs. They note the study only reaches 9B parameters.
record.recipe_differences: End-to-end native visual-language pre-training with image-text data and held-out multimodal teacher-forcing loss; differs from text-only language-model scaling setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Loss behavior varies with the component being scaled, fixed LLM size, training-data size, and visual-encoder depth/width. The paper defines optimal encoder size using a λ = 1% loss-difference criterion.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal visual-encoder size, defined by a 1% loss-difference threshold, grows log-linearly with LLM size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In native MLLMs, the compute-useful visual-encoder size scales as a power of LLM size.

fits_no_version.finding: LLM initialization and modality-specific MoE each reach a given validation loss with about 10x less multimodal data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization and MoE shift the data-scaling curve of native MLLMs by roughly an order of magnitude in data efficiency.

record.problems: The paper states that its scaling study only reaches 9B parameters and calls for validation at larger scales. The scaling figures provide no uncertainty estimates or fitted exponents in the text, and many plotted loss values are not stated numerically.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream benchmark tables and qualitative attention visualizations were not included because they do not test the stated loss-scaling versions. Cited results from other studies were also excluded.

untested.parts: No text-only LM pretraining loss; all losses are multimodal and the LLMs are initialized from pretrained checkpoints.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation. The encoder-vs-LLM size relation (R23) is a different quantity.
Only visual-encoder depth/width at 600M; LLM shape is not varied.
Other modalities (video, speech), repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer scaling; no fitted exponents.
No relation between downstream scores and scale or loss is quantified.
No comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules or data choices.

missing.what: Zero-shot captioning (CIDEr) vs data for init vs scratch. The scratch model 'continues to lag behind' even with more data, hinting that loss and downstream diverge across setups.
Captioning CIDEr across encoder depth/width. Shallower encoders lead in loss early, while deeper encoders are slightly better on captioning, a loss vs downstream mismatch.

record.verdict_notes: All loss evidence is figure-only, with no fitted exponents or uncertainty. The LLM-size sweep covers three points over about 14x, so support for V5 is weak. V7 links were removed from R11–R22: saturation from a bottlenecked component is not fit-dependence. The encoder diminishing returns occur when the LLM is the bottleneck, a condition the original power-law claim already excludes, so they limit rather than challenge V5. The Fig 4 caption and text disagree on which extreme configurations are worse.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports loss trends with model size and training data, but does not report fitted power-law exponents or establish the power-law form across several orders of magnitude for each scaling variable.
No test of predictions from fits on small runs to substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison of parameter and token allocations or compute-optimal parameter/token exponents.
Tests visual-encoder depth and width at a fixed parameter count, not all architecture details or architectures of the language model.
Tests native visual-language models; does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning scaling, or transfer scaling.
Benchmark comparisons are reported, but no relationship between downstream results and scale or pretraining loss is tested.
Does not compare fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, or training schedules, and does not show that published exponents disagree because of those choices.

rows.subject: LLM scaling sweep
rows.size_stated: LLM sizes {0.5B, 1.8B, 7B}; visual encoder fixed at 600M
rows.operation_detail: Scaled LLM parameter size while using the same visual encoder.
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: figure only; text states loss decreases linearly as parameter size increases exponentially, and calls the pattern consistent with conventional LLM scaling
rows.note: The paper describes the trend as log-linear with LLM size; it does not give fitted coefficients or exact loss values in the text.
rows.check: Multimodal image-text loss from LLM-initialized native MLLMs, so it bears on V5, not V1 (text LM loss). Only three LLM sizes spanning about 14x, not several orders of magnitude. The text says 'decreases log-linearly'; the y-axis is labeled log scale. No fitted exponent.

rows.subject: Native MLLM without LLM initialization
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss as multimodal training data size increased.
rows.baseline: LLM-initialized model; comparable loss requires over 10x more data for the model trained from scratch
rows.value: figure only; text says the scratch-trained model performs significantly worse
rows.note: The comparison reports a data-efficiency difference, not a fitted power law.
rows.check: A design comparison (LLM init vs scratch) on data efficiency. It does not test power-law form or any version; no fit reported.

rows.subject: Native MLLM with pre-trained LLM initialization
rows.stage_stated: Native multimodal pre-training; initialized from InternLM2-Base
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss as multimodal training data size increased.
rows.baseline: Scratch-trained model; over 10x more data required by that model to reach comparable loss
rows.value: figure only; text says the initialized model converges much faster
rows.note: Reports data-scaling behavior but does not fit or establish a power-law form.
rows.check: Comparator for the init vs scratch design choice; not a test of a scaling-law version.

rows.subject: Native MLLM without MoE
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across training data sizes for the vanilla LLM configuration.
rows.baseline: MoE-extended configuration; same validation loss reached with 1/10 of the data when using MoE
rows.value: figure only
rows.note: The comparison shows data-efficiency differences, not a fitted power law.
rows.check: MoE vs vanilla design comparison ('1/10 of the data'). Total parameter count differs, so it is not a V4 shape test either.

rows.subject: Native MLLM with MoE
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across training data sizes for the MoE-extended configuration.
rows.baseline: Without MoE; same validation loss reached using 1/10 as much data with MoE
rows.value: figure only; text says MoE causes loss to decrease more quickly
rows.note: The paper reports faster convergence, not a fitted power law.
rows.check: Comparator for the MoE design choice; not a scaling-law test.

rows.subject: Visual encoder configuration d=3
rows.size_stated: Visual encoder parameter count fixed at 600M
rows.operation_detail: Varied visual-encoder depth and adjusted width to maintain the fixed parameter count.
rows.baseline: Other tested depth/width configurations at the same parameter count
rows.value: figure only; text says extremely shallow configurations perform worse
rows.note: The text does not map individual widths to individual depths.
rows.check: Extreme configuration (d3/w4096) is worse. This lies outside V4's 'wide range', so it bounds that range rather than contradicting it. The Fig 4 caption says loss differs only when 'extremely wide or shallow', while the text says both extremes are worse.

rows.subject: LLM-0.5B native MLLM visual-encoder sweep
rows.operation_detail: Scaled visual-encoder size with LLM size held fixed.
rows.baseline: 75M visual encoder; loss with that encoder is the reference in the optimal-size criterion
rows.value: figure only; text reports diminishing gains and a threshold beyond which further scaling gives marginal loss reduction
rows.note: The paper states that the loss gap narrows toward zero at a sufficient encoder size as training data increases.
rows.check: Encoder scaling with a fixed LLM shows diminishing returns. The LLM is a bottleneck here, which the power-law claim excludes. This does not bear on V7 (no fitting-choice comparison), so V7 is removed. R12–R22 share the same fix.

rows.subject: Native MLLM visual-encoder/LLM scaling study
rows.operation_detail: Identified an optimal encoder size for each LLM size using the stated loss-difference threshold.

conditions.value: Smallest encoder whose loss difference from an encoder twice its size is less than λ = 1% of loss with the 75M encoder

rows.measure: Relationship between optimal visual-encoder size and LLM size
rows.baseline: not stated
rows.value: figure only; text says the logarithm of optimal visual-encoder size scales linearly with the logarithm of LLM size
rows.note: This is an encoder-size versus LLM-size relationship, not a fixed-compute parameter/token allocation.

relationships.condition: Scaling the LLM (0.5B, 1.8B, 7B) with a fixed 600M visual encoder in native image-text pre-training
relationships.reason: The authors report loss falling log-linearly with LLM size, 'consistent with the conventional LLM scaling law'. This rests on only three points over about 14x and no fit (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Loss reportedly decreased log-linearly with language-model size across three measurements spanning approximately fourteenfold variation, without a fitted law.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Scaling the LLM (0.5B, 1.8B, 7B) with a fixed 600M visual encoder in native image-text pre-training
source_check.reason: R1 matches the authors' stated conventional scaling pattern in Figure 5, whose loss axis is logarithmic; evidence covers only three sizes without a fitted exponent.

relationships.condition: Scaling only the visual encoder (75M–2.4B) with a fixed LLM, across 15M–120M data
relationships.reason: Gains diminish and become marginal beyond a threshold that depends on LLM size, so encoder parameters do not follow a single power law (R11–R22).
relationships.display_finding: Gains diminished and became marginal beyond an encoder-size threshold that depended on language-model size, departing from a single power law.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Scaling only the visual encoder (75M–2.4B) with a fixed LLM, across 15M–120M data
source_check.reason: R11–R22 capture diminishing encoder-scaling gains and marginal improvement beyond a capacity-dependent threshold. This qualifies independent component scaling; it is not a fitted rejection of every power-law form.

relationships.condition: Visual-encoder depth 6–24 (width adjusted) at a fixed 600M parameters
relationships.reason: Moderate configurations reach 'near-optimal performance across a wide range'; only extreme depth/width settings are worse, consistent with V4's range qualifier (R7–R9, bounded by R6, R10).
relationships.display_finding: Moderate depth-width configurations achieved near-optimal performance across a wide range, while extreme configurations performed worse.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Visual-encoder depth 6–24 (width adjusted) at a fixed 600M parameters
source_check.reason: R7–R9 agree with the near-optimal performance reported across moderate shapes; the extreme configurations in R6 and R10 bound that range.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

source_check.notes: The 75M encoder supplies the reference loss for the optimality criterion in Section 3.3.2, rather than a common plotted endpoint in Figure 6.
